# Inline visual formats - choosing and using each one

The format-selection layer: which renderable format to reach for, and the key craft and gotchas of each. The quality bar (graphical integrity, perceptual effectiveness, the accessibility floor) is in `principles.md` and applies whatever the format. Deep craft for the two primary formats is in `svg-craft.md` (hand-authored SVG) and `interactive.md` (HTML widgets and charting libraries).

## Which format for which job

| The visual is | Reach for | Why |
|---------------|-----------|-----|
| A diagram, badge, or small static chart (few data points) you can enumerate as shapes | Hand-authored **SVG** | Theme-reactive, crisp at any size, no runtime JS, accessible and inspectable |
| A process, architecture, or relationship graph with many nodes, or one that changes often | **Mermaid** (diagram-as-code) | Auto-layout beats hand-routing edges; renders inline in markdown; diffs cleanly |
| A data chart with axes, scales, legends, or many series | A **charting library** in an HTML widget | Hand-authoring axis and tick math is error-prone; libraries handle scales and interaction |
| Data the reader should explore (hover, zoom, filter) | An **interactive HTML widget** | Details-on-demand needs runtime behavior |
| Exact values, mixed units, or a small lookup | A **Markdown table** | A table beats a chart when readers look up or compare individual values |
| A formula or mathematical relationship | **Math** (KaTeX / MathML, `$...$`) | The relationship itself is the content |
| Something inherently geographic | A **map** (GeoJSON via D3-geo or Observable Plot) | Only when geography is the question; otherwise a bar or table is more precise |
| A word-sized magnitude in a list or a plain-text surface | **Unicode** block-element sparkline | When the medium is text-only and a real chart cannot render |

Default to the simplest format that carries the meaning. A static SVG or a table beats an interactive widget whenever exploration is not the point.

## Hand-authored SVG (the primary format)

Best for diagrams, flowcharts, architecture and state diagrams, badges, icons, annotated illustrations, and small bar/line/pie charts with a handful of points: anything enumerable as shapes that must be theme-reactive and crisp with no runtime JS ([CSS-Tricks, scale SVG](https://css-tricks.com/scale-svg/)). Renders inline anywhere SVG is allowed. Fully craftable for accessibility and dark mode. Full craft in `svg-craft.md`. Reach past it to a charting library when data is dynamic or dense and needs axes, scales, legends, or tooltips, since SVG text does not wrap and tick math is error-prone by hand ([MDN, SVG text](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Element/text)).

## Interactive HTML widgets and charting libraries

Best for data charts with axes and for visuals the reader should explore. Build a self-contained single file with inline CSS and JS; many inline and sandboxed renderers block external scripts, so prefer dependency-free or inlined code, and when loading a CDN library use Subresource Integrity ([MDN, SRI](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity)). Library selection, the canvas-versus-SVG crossover, responsive sizing, and interaction patterns are in `interactive.md`.

## Diagram-as-code (Mermaid and alternatives)

**Mermaid** is the diagram-as-code format that renders inline in markdown (GitHub since 2022, Obsidian, many chat UIs) via a fenced ` ```mermaid ` block ([Mermaid intro](https://mermaid.js.org/intro/); [GitHub diagrams](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/working-with-advanced-formatting/creating-diagrams)). It covers flowchart, sequence, class, state, entity-relationship, gantt, pie, mindmap, timeline, gitgraph, and more. Prefer it over hand-SVG when topology is large or generated, when the diagram changes often (text diffs cleanly), or when it must render inline in markdown. Prefer hand-SVG when the diagram is a designed artifact needing pixel-precise layout and full color control.

Clean-Mermaid checklist:
- Pick direction by shape: `TD`/`TB` for hierarchies and decision trees, `LR` for pipelines and process flows.
- Group with `subgraph id [title] ... end`; note that if a subgraph node links outside, its internal `direction` is ignored.
- Reduce crossings: keep flow one-directional and declare nodes in flow order.
- Encode meaning in edge type: `-->` normal, `-.->` dotted (optional or async), `==>` thick (primary path); label edges sparingly.
- Style via `classDef` and `class ...:::name`, not per-node inline styles; target a link with `linkStyle`.
- Theme with `%%{init: {'theme':'base'}}%%` then `themeVariables` (`primaryColor`, `lineColor`, `fontFamily`); the five built-in themes are default, neutral, dark, forest, and base, and base is the customizable one ([Mermaid theming](https://mermaid.js.org/config/theming.html)).
- Always add `accTitle:` and `accDescr:` for the accessible title and description ([Mermaid accessibility](https://mermaid.js.org/config/accessibility.html)).

Alternatives, none of which render natively in markdown (they need a build step or plugin): **Graphviz/DOT** has best-in-class auto-layout for large or dense graphs (`dot` for hierarchies, `sfdp` for big force-directed graphs) ([Graphviz layouts](https://graphviz.org/docs/layouts/)); **D2** produces polished modern architecture diagrams with themes, sketch mode, and automatic dark mode ([d2lang.com](https://d2lang.com/)); **PlantUML** has the broadest UML coverage ([plantuml.com](https://plantuml.com/)).

## Markdown tables

A table communicates better than a chart when readers look up individual values, compare individual values rather than a whole series, need precise numbers, mix more than one unit, or want summary and detail together (Stephen Few, *Show Me the Numbers*; [Few, Effective Chart Design](https://www.perceptualedge.com/images/Effective_Chart_Design.pdf)). Use GitHub-Flavored-Markdown syntax: a header row, a delimiter row (`:---` left, `---:` right, `:---:` center), then data rows, with a blank line before the table ([GFM spec](https://github.github.com/gfm/)). Make it beautiful: right-align numeric columns so decimals line up, left-align text, keep headers terse, and stay near 3 to 6 columns so it does not wrap on narrow surfaces. The header row gives screen readers row and column relationships, so a real table is also the recommended text alternative for a complex chart or map. Gotchas: no block content, rowspan, colspan, nested tables, or multi-line cells; escape literal pipes as `\|`.

## Unicode and ASCII text-art

For a word-sized magnitude beside a number, or any genuinely text-only surface where SVG cannot render. The lower eighth-blocks U+2581 to U+2588 (`one eighth block` to `full block`) give eight steps of vertical resolution for inline bar charts and sparklines; the left eighth-blocks do the same horizontally for progress bars; Braille Patterns (U+2800 to U+28FF) pack a 2x4 dot grid per character for the densest text plots ([Block Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Elements); [Braille Patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille_Patterns)). This requires a monospace font with the glyphs, or the bars smear out of alignment. Always pair the art with the literal value (`▇▇▅ 73%`) because screen readers may announce these code points as gibberish. Use it only when a real chart or table cannot render; otherwise it is a crutch.

## Math

Show a formula when the relationship or definition itself is the content; chart it when you are showing how the quantity behaves. Convention is `$...$` inline and `$$...$$` display (own line, centered); GitHub renders both in markdown, and many chat UIs render via KaTeX ([GitHub math](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/working-with-advanced-formatting/writing-mathematical-expressions)). **KaTeX** renders synchronously with no page reflow and ships a small bundle, but covers fewer LaTeX features; **MathJax** has broader LaTeX coverage and stronger accessibility (exploration and voicing). KaTeX was historically faster, but MathJax 3 has largely closed that gap, so choose KaTeX for synchronous rendering and light weight, MathJax for coverage and accessibility ([KaTeX](https://katex.org/); [MathJax](https://www.mathjax.org/)). Native **MathML Core** reached cross-browser Baseline in January 2023, so dependency-free, semantic math is now viable ([MDN, MathML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/MathML)). Prefer display mode for tall constructs; keep inline math short; escape literal `$`.

## Maps

Reach for a map only when geography is the question (spatial clustering, adjacency, region-to-region pattern); if you are ranking magnitudes, a bar or table is more precise, because a choropleth distorts perceived magnitude by region area. Data is **GeoJSON** (RFC 7946: coordinate order is longitude then latitude, default CRS WGS 84 in decimal degrees) or **TopoJSON** (shares boundaries as arcs for much smaller files) ([RFC 7946](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7946.html)). Render with **D3-geo** (`geoPath` turns GeoJSON into SVG paths) or **Observable Plot**'s `geo` mark (choropleth via `fill`, projection via the `projection` option) ([d3-geo](https://d3js.org/d3-geo); [Observable Plot geo](https://observablehq.com/plot/marks/geo)). Use an equal-area projection (Albers, Equal Earth) when comparing magnitudes across regions, never raw Mercator. The lon-then-lat order is the classic bug. Accessibility is hardest for maps: always provide a data-table alternative.

## Sources

- W3C and MDN: SVG text and SRI, MathML Baseline. CSS-Tricks, scale SVG.
- Mermaid official docs (intro, theming, accessibility); Graphviz, D2, PlantUML official docs; GitHub and Obsidian markdown docs.
- GFM table spec; Stephen Few, *Show Me the Numbers* and *Effective Chart Design*.
- Unicode Block Elements and Braille Patterns; KaTeX, MathJax, MDN MathML; GeoJSON RFC 7946, d3-geo, Observable Plot.
visualize.references/inline-aesthetics.md:
# Inline aesthetics and native feel

What makes an inline visual beautiful and feel like a native part of the conversation, across every format. This is the aesthetic craft layer. The quality standard (graphical integrity, perceptual effectiveness) and the WCAG accessibility floor with its exact contrast numbers live in `principles.md` and are enforced by the Design Critic; this reference does not repeat them, it adds the typography, color, layout, and motion craft.

## Typography

- Use a restrained type scale and only two weights: a normal weight (400 to 500) for body and labels, and one heavier weight for emphasis. Build hierarchy through size, weight, and color, not by piling on weights. To de-emphasize, use a lighter color or smaller size, not a thinner weight ([Refactoring UI, color](https://refactoringui.com/previews/building-your-color-palette/)).
- Prefer sentence case over Title Case or ALL CAPS, everywhere including chart labels and diagram headings. Sentence case is the most readable and is the modern UI standard ([Every Interaction, title vs sentence case](https://www.everyinteraction.com/articles/title-case-vs-sentence-case-in-ui/)).
- Use a system font stack (`system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, sans-serif`) so nothing has to download and the visual matches the host platform.

## Color and theming

- Use flat, restrained palettes: reserve color for emphasis, hold to roughly two or three hues plus grays, and de-emphasize the surrounding elements rather than over-saturating the focal one ([Refactoring UI, building your color palette](https://refactoringui.com/previews/building-your-color-palette/)).
- Theme via CSS custom properties and `currentColor` so a visual inherits the host text color and adapts on its own; support dark mode with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, and use the `color-scheme` property for embedded SVG or iframes ([MDN, prefers-color-scheme](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-color-scheme)).
- For categorical data use a colorblind-safe qualitative ramp: Okabe-Ito's eight colors `#E69F00 #56B4E9 #009E73 #F0E442 #0072B2 #D55E00 #CC79A7 #000000`, distinguishable under the common color-vision deficiencies and distinct in grayscale ([Okabe-Ito guide](https://vizcept.com/blog/okabe-ito-palette-guide)). For continuous data use a perceptually uniform sequential map (viridis, or magma, plasma, inferno), uniform even in black and white, or a ColorBrewer scheme ([viridis](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/viridis/vignettes/intro-to-viridis.html)).
- Never carry meaning by color alone: back semantic color with a redundant label, icon, shape, or pattern (this is the WCAG 1.4.1 rule enforced via `principles.md`).
- The concrete palette library to pick from (categorical, sequential, and diverging, with colorblind-safe defaults) is in `palette.md` and `assets/palettes.json`.

## Layout and signal-scarcity

- Build on a grid: align elements, give generous whitespace, and keep the piece compact so it sits cleanly in a chat bubble.
- Establish hierarchy through size, weight, and color, and actively de-emphasize secondary content so the focal point wins.
- Stay sparse. Emphasis is zero-sum: if everything is emphasized, nothing is. Remove competing elements rather than adding accents ([NN/g, clutter-free charts](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/clutter-charts/)).

## Data-ink and minimalism

Maximize the data-ink ratio, the share of ink that encodes information: erase non-data ink (decorative gridlines, frames, tick clutter, fills) and redundant data ink, within reason ([Tufte, data-ink](https://usefuldatatips.com/tips/visualization/data-ink-ratio)). Stephen Few operationalizes this for screens: remove non-data pixels (borders, fill colors, gradients, 3D, non-essential gridlines) and enhance the data pixels. Gradients, drop shadows, and 3D are chartjunk; flat surfaces read as native.

## Motion (interactive pieces only)

- Keep transitions short and standard: Material specifies about 150 to 200 ms for small transitions, with easing that decelerates longer than it accelerates ([Material, duration and easing](https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/easing-and-duration)). Motion should clarify a change, never decorate.
- Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`: inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, gate or replace scaling and panning animations (for example, swap a scaling pulse for an opacity fade) ([MDN, prefers-reduced-motion](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion)).

## Native feel versus failure modes

Native feel is a flat, compact extension of the conversation: flat surfaces with no gradients, shadows, or noise; colors host-matched via `currentColor` or custom properties; sentence-case, two-weight type; right-sized to the bubble; high data-ink; and a text alternative present.

The failure modes, each the inverse of a rule above:
- Chartjunk and overcrowding (violates data-ink and signal-scarcity).
- Low contrast below the floor in `principles.md` (violates WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11).
- Oversized or broken rendering that overflows the bubble.
- Gradients, drop shadows, and 3D that break flatness.
- Color-only encoding with no redundant cue.
- Explanatory prose stuffed inside the graphic instead of in the chat text or the description: it is non-data ink and invisible to assistive tech. Text goes in the response; the visual carries the visual.

## Sources

- Refactoring UI (color and typography); Every Interaction and USAGov (sentence case); EightShapes (typography in design systems).
- MDN: prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion. Material Design (duration and easing).
- Okabe-Ito palette guide; viridis (CRAN); ColorBrewer. Nielsen Norman Group (clutter-free charts).
- Tufte (data-ink ratio); Stephen Few (information dashboard design).

# Interactive HTML widgets and charting libraries

How to build a self-contained interactive widget and which charting library to reach for. Use this when the visual is a data chart with axes, or one the reader should explore (hover, zoom, filter). When exploration is not the point, a static SVG (`svg-craft.md`) or a table is better. Interaction is governed by `principles.md` (overview first, then detail) and `inline-aesthetics.md` (flat, restrained, accessible).

## Self-contained widgets

Build one HTML document carrying its own inline `<style>` and `<script>`, so it renders with zero network dependencies. Many inline and sandboxed renderers (iframe `srcdoc`, CSP-restricted embeds) block external scripts entirely, so a widget that loads a CDN script can simply fail. The safe default is dependency-free, or the library's minified source inlined into the document. When you must load from a CDN, use Subresource Integrity: add `integrity="sha384-..."` and `crossorigin="anonymous"`, so the browser refuses a tampered file ([MDN, SRI](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity)).

## Charting library decision matrix

| Library | Best for | Renders | Weight (approx) | Interactivity | Accessibility |
|---------|----------|---------|-----------------|---------------|---------------|
| **Chart.js** | Fast standard charts (line, bar, pie) with little config | Canvas | ~80 KB gzip full, tree-shakeable | Hover, tooltip, animation built in | Manual: canvas is opaque, add `role="img"` plus a label or fallback |
| **D3.js** | Bespoke, fully custom, novel visuals | SVG (also canvas) | ~90 KB gzip full, tiny modular | Build-your-own via DOM events | Strong: SVG nodes are inspectable and labelable |
| **Vega-Lite** | Declarative JSON specs, quick exploratory charts | SVG or canvas | heavier (ships Vega runtime) | First-class selections, pan, zoom | SVG mode helps |
| **ECharts** | Large datasets, dashboards, many chart types | Canvas plus SVG | ~100 KB gzip tree-shaken | Rich: dataZoom, brush, tooltip, legend | Best out of the box: auto ARIA descriptions |
| **Plotly.js** | Scientific, statistical, 3D, publication quality | SVG plus WebGL | heaviest, ~2 MB plus | Zoom, pan, hover built in | Partial; SVG inspectable |
| **Observable Plot** | Concise exploratory charts, grammar of graphics | SVG | light, built on D3 | Lighter than ECharts or Plotly | SVG-based |

Reach for **Chart.js** for a quick standard chart, **Observable Plot** or **Vega-Lite** for concise declarative charts, **ECharts** for a dense dashboard with built-in interaction and the best default accessibility, **D3** only when you need something bespoke no library gives, and **Plotly** for scientific or 3D work where its weight is justified. Chart.js renders on canvas; D3, Observable Plot, and Vega-Lite (in SVG mode) render inspectable SVG ([Chart.js](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/); [D3](https://d3js.org/); [Observable Plot](https://observablehq.com/plot/); [ECharts features](https://echarts.apache.org/en/feature.html)).

## Canvas versus SVG

SVG puts every shape in the DOM, so it slows as node count climbs into the thousands; the practical rule is to start with SVG and switch to canvas around a few thousand elements (hardware-dependent, an order-of-magnitude rule, not a hard number) ([JointJS, SVG vs canvas](https://www.jointjs.com/blog/svg-versus-canvas)). The accessibility tradeoff is decisive: SVG elements are in the DOM, carry semantics, and are exposed to assistive tech; a `<canvas>` is a single opaque element that exposes nothing but its fallback content. Prefer SVG for small, static, inspectable charts; reach for canvas only when node count genuinely demands it ([MDN, canvas](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Canvas_API/Tutorial/Optimizing_canvas)).

## Responsive sizing

Size to the container, not the viewport, with `ResizeObserver` (observe the wrapper, read `inlineSize`, redraw); guard against feedback loops by deferring mutations with `requestAnimationFrame` ([MDN, ResizeObserver](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ResizeObserver)). For crisp canvas on high-DPI screens, multiply the bitmap by `devicePixelRatio` while keeping the CSS size fixed, then `ctx.scale(dpr, dpr)` ([MDN, devicePixelRatio](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/devicePixelRatio)). Chart.js encodes this: give it a dedicated relatively-positioned container and use `responsive` plus `maintainAspectRatio`, and never put width or height styles directly on the `<canvas>` (it blurs) ([Chart.js responsive](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/configuration/responsive.html)).

## Interaction design

Structure interaction by Shneiderman's mantra: overview first, then zoom and filter, then details on demand ([Shneiderman 1996](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~ben/papers/Shneiderman1996eyes.pdf)). In practice: show the whole shape first, use tooltips and click-to-expand for details, apply progressive disclosure to keep the default view legible, give a sensible default state (no empty or loading dead-ends), and make every control keyboard-focusable and operable. For a canvas chart, add a labeled text or table fallback, since the pixels are opaque to assistive tech ([Chart.js accessibility](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/general/accessibility.html)).

## Performance and failure modes

- A heavy library inlined balloons the document (Plotly is multi-megabyte); a single chart rarely justifies it.
- Oversized canvases: scale up with CSS transforms rather than allocating a huge bitmap, disable transparency when unused, avoid `shadowBlur`, batch draws, and use `requestAnimationFrame` ([MDN, optimizing canvas](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Canvas_API/Tutorial/Optimizing_canvas)).
- Layout thrash: a `ResizeObserver` callback that mutates the observed element loops; defer with `requestAnimationFrame`.
- Too many SVG nodes: DOM repaint cost climbs past a few thousand elements; move to canvas.

## When interactive versus static

- Interactive HTML widget: the data rewards exploration (hover for details, zoom or filter dense or multi-series data, what-if controls).
- Static SVG: a fixed, small-node chart that must be inspectable, labelable, and dependency-free. Best for accessibility and reliable inline embedding.
- Static raster image: only when scripts are blocked and the visual will never need interaction, or node counts would choke the DOM.

## Sources

- Official docs: Chart.js (and its responsive and accessibility pages), D3, Vega-Lite, ECharts, Plotly.js, Observable Plot.
- MDN: ResizeObserver, devicePixelRatio, Subresource Integrity, optimizing canvas.
- Shneiderman, "The Eyes Have It," 1996; JointJS (SVG vs canvas).

# Color palettes - the library and how to pick one

The skill ships a curated library of the most established data-visualization palettes (about 87) in `assets/palettes.json`, drawn verbatim from the canonical sources: ColorBrewer, the viridis family (matplotlib), Tableau, D3, Plotly, CARTOColors, Paul Tol, and Okabe-Ito. The Visualization Designer picks one palette per visual at creation, matched to the data; the Design Critic still enforces the accessibility gate on the choice. This reference is how to choose and apply; the colors live in the asset.

## Pick by data type first

The palette type is decided by what the data IS, not by what looks nice. `palettes.json` is split into the three types for exactly this reason.

- **categorical** (qualitative): distinct, unordered series with no ranking. Bars grouped by category, multi-line charts (one hue per line), pie or donut slices, maps of discrete classes. Color encodes identity, so hues must be maximally distinct with no implied order.
- **sequential**: ordered data running low to high in one direction. Heatmaps, choropleths of one quantity, density, counts. More reads as darker or more saturated. Color encodes amount.
- **diverging**: data with a meaningful midpoint and two directions away from it. Deviation from zero or a mean, surplus and deficit, correlation, z-scores, change. The neutral center marks the reference value; the two saturated ends mark the extremes. Align the data's reference point to the palette's midpoint, or the visual misleads.

## Prefer a colorblind-safe default

Unless a specific look is requested, default to a colorblind-safe palette (the `cvd_safe_defaults` block in the asset):

- **categorical:** Okabe-Ito (8 colors, the safest qualitative default), Tol Bright or Tol Muted, or Tableau Color Blind 10. Each was engineered and tested against red-green deficiency.
- **sequential:** viridis (perceptually uniform, monotonic lightness, legible under all color-vision deficiencies and in grayscale) or cividis (optimized for deficiency). Monotonic lightness is what keeps the order readable even when hue discrimination fails.
- **diverging:** ColorBrewer RdBu or BrBG, or Tol sunset. Two arms on opposite, distinguishable hue axes with a light neutral center.

A palette flagged `cvd_safe: false` (Set1, Spectral, Material, most Plotly and CARTO sets) is for when beauty or a specific brand mood outranks strict accessibility, and only after the Critic confirms the encoding still passes contrast and is not color-only.

## How to apply

- **categorical:** assign the palette's colors to series in order. Cap distinct series at about 8; Okabe-Ito and Tol Bright top out there because more hues stop being reliably distinguishable. Beyond 8, group the long tail into an "other" bucket, use small multiples, or direct-label the series instead of a color legend.
- **sequential:** map the ordered values across the ramp low to high; use the ramp's stops or interpolate between them for a continuous scale.
- **diverging:** put the data's zero or reference at the palette's neutral center, and scale the two arms symmetrically so equal deviations read as equal color distance.

## Palette for data, host tokens for chrome

The palette colors the data marks (bars, lines, slices, regions). The visual's chrome (text, axes, gridlines, borders) should still use the host theme via `currentColor` and CSS variables so it adapts to light and dark (see `svg-craft.md` and `inline-aesthetics.md`). Do not hardcode a palette color for text or axes. A categorical palette is for the series, not the frame.

## The Critic still gates

Picking from this library does not bypass the accessibility gate. The Design Critic checks the chosen palette in context: text and meaningful-graphics contrast meet the WCAG floor in `principles.md`, information is never carried by color alone (pair with labels, shapes, or direct labeling), and for multi-series categorical work the adjacent colors are actually distinguishable at the rendered size. A beautiful palette that fails these is sent back, not shipped.

## Sources

All hex in `assets/palettes.json` was copied verbatim from canonical sources and uppercased: ColorBrewer (colorbrewer2.org), the viridis family and coolwarm (matplotlib / the BIDS colormap project), Tableau's palette reference, d3-scale-chromatic, Plotly's qualitative color modules, CARTOColors (the CartoColor repo), Paul Tol's technical note, and the Okabe-Ito Color Universal Design set.

# Visualization principles - the durable craft knowledge

The doctrine the Design team works to, grounded in the established authorities. Read before the critique gate. The one standard is **graphical integrity**: the visual never distorts what is true. The craft rule beneath it is **legible and accessible**.

## Form by question (the Lead picks first)

The single highest-leverage call. Choose the form from the question and the data, before anything is drawn.

| The question is about | Form | Notes |
|-----------------------|------|-------|
| Comparison of values across categories | Bar or column | Sorted by value unless the order is inherent (time). Zero baseline. |
| A trend over ordered time | Line | Lines are compared to each other, so a non-zero axis is acceptable if clearly labeled. |
| Correlation between two variables | Scatter | Add a trend line only when it is honest. |
| Part-to-whole | Stacked bar, rarely a pie | A pie only for 2 to 3 slices; a sorted bar reads ranking better. |
| A process or decision logic | Flowchart | One flow direction; label decision branches. |
| Static structure or components | Architecture or entity diagram | Group by subsystem; minimize crossings. |
| Object interaction over time | Sequence diagram | Time down the page; actors across the top. |
| Events along time | Timeline | Consistent scale; label the events, not the gaps. |
| Exploration of many values | Interactive | Overview first, then zoom and filter, then details. |
| A concept or mechanism | Explanatory illustration | One visual language; semantic, not decorative. |

## Graphical integrity (Tufte)

- **Lie factor** = (size of the effect shown in the graphic) / (size of the effect in the data). Honest is near 1. A truncated bar axis or a distorted area inflates it.
- **Proportionality.** The geometry on the page is proportional to the numbers. Bars encode value by length, so the baseline starts at zero; clipping it is the most common lie.
- **Data-ink ratio.** Maximize the share of ink that encodes data; erase decorative grids, heavy frames, and redundant ink.
- **Chartjunk.** Remove ornament that encodes nothing: 3D, moire grids, gratuitous pictograms.
- **Forbidden by default:** truncated or non-zero baselines on bars; dual y-axes (they manufacture spurious correlation); 3D effects (perspective distorts magnitude); area or bubble encoding of a single quantity (radius-versus-area ambiguity).

## Perceptual effectiveness

- **Cleveland and McGill ranking** of how accurately people decode a channel, most to least: position on a common scale; position on nonaligned scales; length, direction, and angle (one rank together); area; volume and curvature; color shading and saturation. Encode the most important quantity with the highest channel available. This is why bars and dot plots beat pies (angle) and bubbles (area).
- **Munzner's effectiveness principle:** match the importance of an attribute to the salience of its channel; the most important attribute gets the most effective channel.
- **Preattentive attributes** (hue, size, orientation) let a viewer spot a target in under about 250 ms without serial search; use one, not five, to mark what matters.
- **Bertin's visual variables** (position, size, shape, value, color, orientation, texture) are the encoding vocabulary.

## Gestalt grouping (especially diagrams and dashboards)

The eye groups marks by **proximity** (nearness), **similarity** (shared color or shape), **enclosure** (a shared border or shaded region), **connectedness** (linked elements read as one, the strongest cue), and **continuity and closure**. Lay panels and clusters out so the grouping the eye sees matches the relationships in the data.

## Accessibility (WCAG 2.2, the blocking floor)

- **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), AA:** text at least **4.5:1**; large text at least **3:1**, where large is **18 point, or 14 point bold**.
- **1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, AA:** UI components and the parts of graphics required to understand the content at least **3:1** against adjacent colors (not rounded; 2.99:1 fails).
- **1.4.1 Use of Color, A:** color is never the only means of conveying information; pair it with a label, a pattern, or direct labeling.
- **1.1.1 Non-text Content, A:** every chart or diagram carries a text alternative.
- **Palettes:** Okabe-Ito for categorical (color-vision-deficiency-safe and distinct in grayscale); viridis or ColorBrewer for sequential and continuous data.

## Interactive and dashboards

- **Shneiderman's visual information-seeking mantra:** "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand." The overview is the first thing seen and guides the rest.
- **Stephen Few:** a dashboard fits a single screen; avoid clutter, meaningless variety, excessive precision, and inaccurate encoding. Surface the headline; do not make the user dig for it.
- **Progressive disclosure:** show the primary view by default; reveal depth on request, with discoverable, labeled, keyboard-reachable controls.

## Mode do's and don'ts (the high-leverage few)

- **Charts:** start bars at zero; match the chart type to the task; encode with position and length; sort and direct-label. Do not use a pie for more than 2 to 3 slices, dual y-axes, 3D, or a truncated bar axis.
- **Diagrams:** one flow direction; minimize edge crossings (the single most validated readability lever); conventional, consistent shapes; label decision branches. Do not space unevenly, over-branch, or color decoratively.
- **Interactive:** overview then zoom and filter then details; a sensible default state; discoverable controls. Do not bury the point or hide essential actions behind obscure affordances.
- **Illustration:** one visual language and abstraction level; semantic clarity over decoration; label what carries meaning. Do not substitute a pretty illustration where precision is required.

## The Critic's checklist (in order)

1. **Form-fit (first).** Is this the right form for the question and the data? Wrong form is FATAL even when the execution is flawless.
2. **Integrity, charts:** zero baseline on bars; lie factor near 1; no 3D, dual axis, or area-encoding of one quantity; chartjunk removed; comparisons on a common scale.
3. **Integrity, diagrams:** every real relationship present and no false one; crossings minimized; flow and hierarchy honest; consistent notation.
4. **Accessibility (blocking, enumerated):** text contrast at least 4.5:1 (3:1 large); non-text at least 3:1; never color alone; a color-vision-deficiency-safe palette; a text alternative present; interactive controls keyboard-reachable and labeled.
5. **Clarity:** one takeaway; the title states the so-what; axes, units, and legends labeled; an interactive supports overview, zoom and filter, and details on demand.

## Sources

- Edward Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (graphical integrity, lie factor, data-ink, chartjunk).
- Cleveland and McGill, "Graphical Perception," JASA, 1984 (the perceptual-accuracy ranking).
- Tamara Munzner, *Visualization Analysis and Design* (the effectiveness principle).
- Jacques Bertin, *Semiology of Graphics* (visual variables).
- Stephen Few, *Information Dashboard Design* (dashboard principles).
- Ben Shneiderman, "The Eyes Have It," 1996 (the visual information-seeking mantra).
- W3C WAI, WCAG 2.2 Understanding documents, success criteria 1.4.3, 1.4.11, 1.4.1, 1.1.1.
- Okabe and Ito, Color Universal Design qualitative palette; viridis and ColorBrewer for sequential schemes.

# SVG craft - beautiful, reliable, theme-reactive hand-authored SVG

Hand-authored SVG is the primary inline format (see `formats.md` for when to use it). This is how to make it beautiful and reliable: it scales crisply, adapts to light and dark, never overflows its text, and carries a text alternative. The aesthetic bar is in `inline-aesthetics.md`; the quality standard is in `principles.md`.

## Setup and scaling

- Set `viewBox`, not pixel `width`/`height`. `viewBox="min-x min-y width height"` maps the user-space rectangle to the rendered element, and all inner coordinates resolve against it ([MDN viewBox](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Attribute/viewBox)). Let the host size it (`width: 100%; height: auto`) so it stays fluid and crisp at any DPI ([CSS-Tricks, scale SVG](https://css-tricks.com/scale-svg/)).
- `preserveAspectRatio` controls fit when the container ratio differs; the default `xMidYMid meet` scales uniformly and keeps the whole graphic visible. It has no effect without a `viewBox`.
- Draw no full-canvas background rect. SVG has no background by default, so it inherits the chat surface and stays transparent.

## Theming for light and dark

- Use `fill="currentColor"` and `stroke="currentColor"` so shapes inherit the host CSS `color` and recolor automatically when the theme flips ([Hidde de Vries, dark-mode SVG](https://hidde.blog/making-single-color-svg-icons-work-in-dark-mode/)).
- A hardcoded fill breaks dark mode. An unstyled or explicitly black shape stays invisibly dark on a dark surface, because the SVG default fill is black and dark-mode engines recolor CSS, not baked-in markup attributes ([MDN fill](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Attribute/fill)).
- For multi-color art, layer CSS custom properties with a `currentColor` fallback: `fill: var(--accent, currentColor)`, and respond to the OS preference with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` ([MDN prefers-color-scheme](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-color-scheme)).

## Markers and arrowheads

Define arrowheads as a `<marker>` in `<defs>` and reference them with `marker-end` (or `marker-start`/`marker-mid`) on a line or path ([MDN marker](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Element/marker)).
- `markerUnits` defaults to `strokeWidth`, so the head scales with line weight.
- `orient="auto-start-reverse"` lets a single marker definition serve both ends pointing outward when it is referenced by both `marker-start` and `marker-end`; it reverses only the start marker, and on `marker-mid`/`marker-end` it otherwise behaves like `auto`.
- Set `fill="context-stroke"` on the marker path so the arrowhead matches the line color and tracks `currentColor` across themes; this is the detail most hand-SVG gets wrong (a black arrowhead on a themed line). `context-stroke` in markers is recent (Chrome and Edge 124, April 2024) and works in current webviews; when broad or older compatibility matters, set the marker's `stroke` and `fill` to `currentColor` directly as the fallback.

## Text that never overflows

SVG `<text>` does not wrap by default; the content area is otherwise treated as infinite ([MDN text](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Element/text); [W3C SVG2 text](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG/text.html)). So:
- Keep labels short and size boxes from estimated text width: budget about 0.55 to 0.6em per character at the chosen font size, plus padding. A 20-character label at 14px is roughly 180px wide, so a box needs about 180 plus 2x the padding.
- Constrain a single line with `textLength` plus `lengthAdjust`. The user agent ensures the text does not extend past that width, which also keeps width stable even if a web font fails to load ([MDN textLength](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Attribute/textLength)). Use `lengthAdjust="spacingAndGlyphs"` only when you accept glyph scaling.
- For multi-line, stack `<tspan>` children with an incremental `dy`. Reserve `foreignObject` (real HTML wrapping) for genuinely long passages; it is a heavier dependency.
- Color text with `fill`, never `color` (the `color` property is for HTML).

## Accessibility

- For a meaningful graphic use `role="img"` on the `<svg>`, a short `<title>` (first child) and a longer `<desc>`, wired with `aria-labelledby="titleID descID"`. The explicit `aria-labelledby` link is the reliable pattern because browser and assistive-tech auto-exposure of bare title and desc is inconsistent ([CSS-Tricks, accessible SVGs](https://css-tricks.com/accessible-svgs/); [Smashing, accessible SVG patterns](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2021/05/accessible-svg-patterns-comparison/)).
- For a purely decorative graphic, add `aria-hidden="true"` ([W3C WAI images](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/)).
- Add `focusable="false"` to avoid stray tab stops in legacy engines.

## Style and the common gotchas

- Stay flat and chartjunk-free: no gradients, drop shadows, or 3D (see `inline-aesthetics.md`).
- Fill inherits through `<g>`, so set color on a group and override only where needed. Beware that `opacity` does not inherit while `fill-opacity` does.
- Keep hairlines crisp under transform scaling with `vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke"` (it applies under `transform`, not plain CSS resize) ([MDN vector-effect](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Attribute/vector-effect)).
- Assume no installed fonts; use a system stack: `font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, sans-serif"`.
- The y axis grows downward; only the `viewBox` clips, so keep stroked shapes inside the box by half the stroke width to avoid edge clipping.

## A minimal setup skeleton

```
<svg viewBox="0 0 W H" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="t d">
  <title id="t">short title</title>
  <desc id="d">one-sentence description of what the visual shows</desc>
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M2 1L8 5L2 9" fill="none" stroke="context-stroke" stroke-width="1.5"
            stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- shapes use fill/stroke="currentColor" or a CSS var; text is short and pre-sized -->
</svg>
```

## Do and don't

- Do set `viewBox` plus fluid sizing; don't hardcode pixel `width`/`height`.
- Do use `currentColor` or CSS vars; don't bake in black or a fixed hex (default fill is black, invisible in dark mode).
- Do give markers `context-stroke` and `orient="auto-start-reverse"`; don't hardcode the arrowhead color.
- Do keep labels short, pre-size boxes, and use `textLength`/`tspan`; don't assume text wraps or a font exists.
- Do add `role="img"` plus `aria-labelledby` to title and desc, or `aria-hidden` if decorative; don't ship an unlabeled meaningful graphic.

## Sources

- MDN SVG references: viewBox, preserveAspectRatio, marker, orient, textLength, text, fill, vector-effect, prefers-color-scheme.
- W3C SVG 2 text spec; W3C WAI images tutorial.
- CSS-Tricks (accessible SVGs, scale SVG); Smashing Magazine (accessible SVG patterns); Hidde de Vries (single-color SVG icons in dark mode).

# Visual brief (the Design Lead fills this before dispatching)

A self-contained brief the Lead writes in Phase 0 and threads into every dispatch, so whichever agent acts works to the real request rather than improvising it.

- **Request:** [what the Founder asked for, verbatim or close]
- **Question the visual must answer:** [the one thing a reader should take away]
- **Data or content:** [the numbers, the structure, or the concept; note the source and whether it is clean]
- **Audience and medium:** [who reads it, where it renders, chat or a saved file]
- **Chosen form and why:** [the single form, with the one-line reason it fits the question, from the form-by-question table in references/principles.md]
- **Integrity constraints:** [zero baseline, honest scale, no forbidden encoding; any data caveat]
- **Accessibility floor:** [contrast, a color-vision-deficiency-safe palette, never color alone, a text alternative]
- **Tier:** [quick | standard | interactive]
- **Home:** [a named save location, or "chat only" if it is a leaving visual]

---
# Part of tannergolden/intelligence's home kit, which replaces this file on every install.
name: reviewer
description: "Reviews a change before it is pushed or merged. Checks the diff against its task, the repository's AGENTS.md and the universal rules, runs the checks itself, and returns verified findings ranked by severity with file and line evidence. Use after a Worker or the main session finishes a change, or whenever the user asks for a review. It never edits files."
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---

You are a Reviewer: you find what is wrong with a change and prove it. You never edit, commit, push or comment, even to fix what you find.

1. Establish the change: the diff against its base branch, and the task it was meant to do. Ask the caller for either one if it is unclear.
2. Read each changed file around the diff, and the repository's AGENTS.md.
3. Run the documented checks yourself. A result someone reports is a claim, not evidence.
4. Look, in this order, for:
   - behaviour that is wrong, or changed without a test;
   - a check weakened to pass: a test deleted, skipped or loosened, or an error suppressed;
   - a credential, a private repository's name or personal context in the diff;
   - work beyond the task;
   - an edit inside an INTELLIGENCE block;
   - where the owner's standards apply: the branch name, the commit messages, and a sign-off from a person.
5. Verify every finding before you report it: trace a real input or command to the failure. Drop what you cannot show.

Report the findings most severe first. Give each one its file and line, what fails, how you showed it, and the smallest fix. If nothing survives, say so plainly and list what you checked.

worker.claude:
---
# Part of tannergolden/intelligence's home kit, which replaces this file on every install.
name: worker
description: "Implements one well-defined change in the current repository and reports back with evidence. Use for a self-contained coding task that fits in a few sentences with its acceptance check, when the main session wants it done in a fresh context and reviewed before anything is pushed."
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, Bash
---

You are a Worker: you make one change, prove it works, and report. The universal rules in your instructions apply to you in full.

1. Read the task, the code around what you will change, and the repository's AGENTS.md, above all its Commands and Definition of done.
2. Make the smallest change that does the task. Leave out anything it does not need: refactors, renames, reformatting, new files and dependencies.
3. Run the checks that cover the change. When one fails, fix the cause; never weaken the check.
4. Never push, open a pull request, comment or publish. The session that called you decides that.
5. If the task can be read two ways that lead to different work, stop and return the question instead of guessing.

Report in this shape, and nothing else:

- Changed: each file, and why.
- Ran: each command, with its output.
- Failed or skipped: what, and why.
- Assumed: anything you decided without being told.
